# Uncovering Unrecognized Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction Among Individuals with Obesity and Dyspnea

**Authors:** Leah B. Kosyakovsky; Elizabeth E. Liu; Jessica K. Wang; Lisa Myers; Juhi K Parekh; Hanna Knauss; Gregory D. Lewis; Rajeev Malhotra; Matthew Nayor; Jeremy M. Robbins; Robert E. Gerszten; Naomi M. Hamburg; Jenna N. McNeill; Emily S. Lau; Jennifer E. Ho

**Affiliations:** 1Division of Cardiology, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA | 2Division of Cardiology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 3Department of Medicine, Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Boston, MA, USA | 4Sections of Cardiology and Preventive Medicine and Epidemiology, Division of Internal Medicine, Boston University School of Medicine, Boston, MA | 5Evans Department of Medicine and Whitaker Cardiovascular Institute, Boston University Chobanian and Avedisian School of Medicine, Boston, MA | 6Division of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA, USA

## Abstract

While heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) has become the predominant HF subtype, it remains clinically underrecognized. HFpEF diagnosis is particularly challenging in the setting of obesity given the limitations of natriuretic peptides and resting echocardiography (TTE). We examined invasive and noninvasive HFpEF diagnostic criteria among individuals with obesity and dyspnea without known cardiovascular disease (CVD) to determine the prevalence of hemodynamic HFpEF in the community.

Research volunteers with dyspnea and obesity underwent resting echocardiogram; participants with possible pulmonary hypertension qualified for invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET). HFpEF was defined using rest or exercise pulmonary capillary wedge pressure criteria (rPCWP ≥15 mm Hg or ΔPCWP/Δ cardiac output slope >2.0 mm Hg·L−1·min−1).

Among n=78 participants (age 53±13 years, 65% women, BMI 37.3±6.8 kg/m2), 40 (51%) met echocardiogram criteria to undergo invasive CPET. In total, 24 participants (60% among CPET group, 31% among total sample) were diagnosed with HFpEF by rPCWP (n=12) or exercise criteria (n=12). There were no differences in NT-proBNP (79 [62, 104] vs 73 [57, 121] pg/mL) or resting echocardiogram (mitral E/e’ ratio 9.1±3.1 vs 8.0±2.7) among those with vs without HFpEF (p>0.05 for all). Distributions of HFpEF diagnostic scores were similar, with the majority classified as intermediate-risk (100% vs 93.75% [H2FPEF] and 87.5% vs 68.75% [HFA-PEFF] in those with vs without HFpEF).

Among adults with obesity and dyspnea without known CVD, at least a third had clinically unrecognized HFpEF uncovered on invasive CPET. Clinical, biomarker, resting echocardiogram, and diagnostic scores were similar among those with and without HFpEF. These results suggest clinical underdiagnosis of HFpEF among individuals with obesity and highlight limitations of noninvasive testing in the identification of HFpEF.

## INTRODUCTION

While heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) represents a steadily increasing proportion of patients with heart failure (HF), it likely remains clinically underrecognized.1,2 The diagnosis of HFpEF remains challenging due to numerous factors, including clinical and phenotypic heterogeneity as well as imperfect diagnostic tools. Recent clinical diagnostic scores incorporating clinical, biomarker, and echocardiographic measures (including the H2FPEF and HFA-PEFF scores) were developed to help risk stratify individuals with suspected HFpEF, though misclassification is common.3,4 Further, under-recognition of HFpEF may be particularly problematic among individuals in whom rest congestion is absent and exercise intolerance or dyspnea is the hallmark symptom.5 This potential for underdiagnosis has underscored the importance of provocative maneuvers including cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET), which may identify hemodynamic abnormalities indicative of HFpEF even in the absence of abnormal diagnostic criteria at rest.3–5 With the evolution of HFpEF therapies, including the recent approval of sodium-glucose transport protein 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors for the treatment of HFpEF, timely diagnosis has important clinical consequences.6

Increasingly, obesity has been recognized as a critical risk factor for the development of HFpEF, affecting up to 80% of all patients with HFpEF,7–9 with recent data suggesting the presence of a distinct, “obese” clinical and hemodynamic HFpEF phenotype.10,11 However, individuals with obesity may be less likely to be clinically diagnosed with HFpEF given the broad, non-cardiac differential diagnosis for their dyspnea, spanning from obesity hypoventilation syndrome to deconditioning, as well as the limitations of volume assessment by physical examination.12 Additionally, N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) values are consistently lower in the setting of obesity, limiting biochemical corroboration of HFpEF diagnosis.10,13 Lastly, echocardiographic assessment may be more challenging in the setting of obesity due to limited acoustic windows, as well as underestimation of circulatory congestion using traditional measures of diastolic function.14

In this study, we sought to investigate the prevalence of clinically unrecognized HFpEF among a sample of adults with obesity and exertional dyspnea without known clinical HFpEF or underlying cardiovascular disease (CVD). We conducted a prospective study of research volunteers who underwent comprehensive clinical assessment, echocardiography (TTE), and CPET with invasive hemodynamic monitoring. We investigated differences in clinical, hemodynamic, and echocardiographic features, as well as diagnostic performance of the H2FPEF and HFA-PEFF scores, among individuals with and without hemodynamic evidence of HFpEF.

## METHODS

### Study sample

The Cardiometabolic Disease and Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing (METCPET) study was a prospective observational study conducted at Massachusetts General Hospital (Figure S1). Briefly, study volunteers were recruited from outpatient primary care clinics and research volunteer websites. Inclusion criteria were age 30–80 years, obesity or overweight (history of BMI ≥ 30 kg/m2 and current BMI ≥ 25 kg/m2), dyspnea (grade ≥1 by modified Medical Research Council scale), and absence of known CVD. Study recruitment was focused on the identification of volunteers with obesity and minimal comorbidities, including an absence of atrial fibrillation, severe pulmonary disease, or renal impairment. Participants underwent comprehensive assessment including clinical examination, resting echocardiogram, and fasting bloodwork. Individuals who meet echocardiographic criteria underwent CPET with invasive hemodynamic monitoring. The study was approved by the appropriate institutional review boards at Massachusetts General Hospital and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. The data that support the findings of this study are available from the corresponding author on reasonable request.

### Clinical, biomarker, and echocardiographic measures

At the first screening visit, study volunteers signed consent and underwent comprehensive medical history, physical examination including anthropometrics, and electrocardiogram. Fasting bloodwork was obtained and immediately processed and stored at −80C until assayed. NT-proBNP was assayed using ELISA (Abcam). Resting echocardiogram was performed and included standard 2-D views and tissue Doppler. Standard echocardiogram measures were reviewed by trained personnel, including left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), LV end diastolic dimension (LVEDD), LV wall thickness, tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP; estimated from both tricuspid regurgitant jet and pulmonary artery acceleration time), left atrial volume index (LAVI), peak early diastolic tissue velocity (e’) at the septal and lateral mitral annulus, and diastolic grade.15 Global longitudinal strain (GLS) was measured using speckle tracking software (Tomtec, Chicago, IL). Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) were used to determine intra- and interobserver variability for GLS with excellent intraobserver (ICC 0.94; 95% CI 0.89–0.96) and interobserver (ICC 0.97; 95% CI 0.93–0.98) agreement.

As our study sample was composed of research volunteers who were not otherwise clinically referred for invasive CPET, we utilized the presence of pulmonary hypertension on resting echocardiogram as a screening tool for participation in invasive testing. Participants with PASP≥40mmHg estimated from pulmonary artery acceleration time (PAAT; measured in triplicate)16 qualified for comprehensive invasive CPET done solely in the context of this research study (n=35). In addition to the research volunteers who qualified on the basis of PASP elevation, n=5 participants with obesity, dyspnea, and no history of HFpEF who were clinically referred for invasive CPET were also included.

### Right heart catheterization and CPET with invasive hemodynamic monitoring

Qualifying participants underwent pulmonary artery catheter insertion via the internal jugular vein with assessment of resting supine hemodynamic measures. CPET with invasive hemodynamic measurements and gas exchange analysis was then performed. Specifically, upright cycle ergometry was performed, which included an initial 3-minute period of unloaded exercise followed by a 5 to 15 W/min continuous ramp protocol to maximal effort.3,17 We assessed breath-by-breath gas exchange using a metabolic cart (MedGraphics, St. Paul, MN) and serial hemodynamic measures including cardiac output (CO) and pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) at rest and at one-minute intervals during exercise. Venous oxygen content was calculated from blood gas samples drawn from the pulmonary artery, whereas arterial oxygen content was estimated from peripheral arterial oxygen saturation.

Cardiac output was calculated using the direct Fick method. Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure (PCWP) tracings were manually reviewed and represented mean values assessed at end-expiration. A diagnosis of HFpEF was made based on either a) rest congestion (supine resting PCWP ≥15 mm Hg) or b) abnormally steep PCWP response indexed to cardiac output calculated from repeated measures at every minute of exercise as previously described (PCWP/CO slope >2.0 mmHg·L−1·min−1).2,3,17 Peak oxygen uptake (VO2) was defined as the highest median measurement obtained during the last minute of exercise, and percent predicted VO2 was calculated for each participant with the Wasserman method using both measured and ideal body weight.18,19 The transpulmonary gradient (TPG) exercise response indexed to CO (ΔTPG/ΔCO slope) was defined as the difference between the mPAP/CO and PCWP/CO slopes. PCWP/CO slope and mPAP/CO measurements were calculated using upright repeated measures at rest and every minute of exercise to peak.

### Statistical analysis

Clinical, echocardiographic, and CPET characteristics were summarized for the total sample and stratified by participants with and without HFpEF diagnostic criteria. Between group differences were ascertained using chi square, two-tailed t-tests, Fisher’s exact tests, or Wilcoxon rank-sum tests as appropriate. We calculated HFA-PEFF20 and H2FPEF21 diagnostic scores for each participant and compared distributions between participants with and without HFpEF. Pulmonary pressures calculated from the tricuspid regurgitation (TR) jet were used for HFpEF risk prediction scores. Analyses were conducted using STATA v17 (StataCorp, College Station, Texas).

## RESULTS

The baseline clinical and echocardiographic characteristics for the total sample (n=78) and the subset of participants who underwent CPET (n=40) are displayed in Table 1. Among the total sample, the mean age was 53±13 years, with 65% women and 71% white race. The mean BMI was 37.3±6.8 kg/m2 with 32 participants (41%) meeting criteria for class 1 obesity (BMI 30 to <35 kg/m2), 16 (21%) for class 2 (BMI 35 to <40 kg/m2), 24 (31%) for class 3 (BMI ≥40 kg/m2), and the remainder (6, 7%) meeting criteria for overweight (BMI 25 to <30 kg/m2) with a prior documented history of obesity. Although no participants had known pre-existing CVD or HFpEF, many had CV risk factors (35% hypertension, 5% diabetes, 35% hyperlipidemia, and 31% OSA). Baseline clinical characteristics were similar among individuals who did and did not qualify for CPET. Of the 40 individuals who underwent invasive CPET, 24 (60% of participants who qualified for CPET, or 31% of the total sample) met diagnostic criteria for HFpEF. Among participants with hemodynamic evidence of HFpEF, half met resting PCWP criteria (n=12), and half met exercise criteria (ΔPCWP/ΔCO slope >2.0 mmHg·L−1·min−1, n=12, Figure 1). In sensitivity analyses, all participants who met ΔPCWP/ΔCO slope criteria also met criteria for absolute upright exercise PCWP≥20 mm Hg (Table S1). Further, after excluding 5 individuals referred in the setting of clinically-indicated CPET, 20 of 35 (57%) research volunteers met hemodynamic HFpEF criteria.

### Clinical and echocardiographic measures among those with and without HFpEF

There were no significant differences in clinical characteristics between n=24 individuals who met HFpEF criteria compared with n=16 who did not (Table 1). Further, NT-proBNP concentrations were similar among participants with and without HFpEF (79 [62, 104] vs 73 [57, 121] pg/mL, p=0.99). Among those with vs without HFpEF, only 2 (8.3%) vs 3 (18.8%) met criteria for elevated NT-proBNP based on a clinical cut-point of ≥125 pg/ml.

With respect to echocardiographic measures of cardiac structure and function, there were no differences in LV wall thickness, left atrial volume, LV mass index, or mitral E/e’ ratio among participants with vs without HFpEF (Table 1), although participants with vs without HFpEF had a higher LV ejection fraction (69±6% vs 62±7%, p=0.004) and relative wall thickness (RWT; 0.50 [0.1] vs 0.43 [0.1], p=0.006). The pulmonary artery systolic pressure (PASP) as estimated from both TR jet (21.9±9.8 vs 21.7±8.9 mmHg, p=0.97) and pulmonary artery acceleration time (49.1±6.2 vs 49.1±4.6 mmHg, p=0.99) were similar between groups. Only 44 participants (56% of the total sample) had a sufficient tricuspid regurgitant jet for PASP determination. GLS was similarly reduced in both groups (−14.8±4.0% vs −15.2±4.0%, p=0.76).

### Exercise capacity and hemodynamic responses among those with and without HFpEF

Participants exercised to maximal effort as measured by the respiratory exchange ratio (RER), which was similar among individuals with and without HFpEF (RER, 1.2±0.1 vs 1.2±0.1, p=0.06; Table 2). Further, overall exercise capacity was similarly impaired in both groups (peak VO2 14.4 ±3.4 vs 14.4 ±3.8ml/kg/min, p=0.98; percent predicted peak VO2 69% [58, 83] vs 64% [54, 84], p=0.47). There were also no significant differences in ventilatory efficiency (VE/VCO2 slope 32.4 ±5.5 vs 32.1 ±5.2, p=0.87).

By definition, hemodynamic measures among those with vs without HFpEF differed, with higher resting supine right atrial pressure (RAP, 9±4 vs 7±3mmHg, p=0.03), mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP, 23±6 vs 18±5mmHg, p=0.005), and PCWP (15±6 vs 10±4mmHg, p=0.001) among those with HFpEF.

With respect to exercise hemodynamic responses, participants with HFpEF had higher RAP (15±6 vs 9±3 mmHg, p<0.001), mPAP (44±12 vs 30±8 mmHg, p<0.001), and PCWP (29±10 vs 15±6 mmHg, p<0.001) with exercise compared with non-HFpEF participants (Figure 2). Mean upright RAP, mPAP, and PCWP measurements were elevated at peak exercise relative to rest for participants with or without HFpEF (all p<0.001, Figure 2 and Table S2). By contrast, rest and peak cardiac output were similar (all p>0.05), as was peripheral O2 extraction (peak C(a-v)O2 12.0±2.1 vs 11.5±1.9 ml/dl , p=0.42, Table 2). Among individuals undergoing CPET, 23/40 (58%) met hemodynamic criteria for resting pulmonary hypertension and an additional 8/40 (20%) met criteria for exercise pulmonary hypertension. There was only a modest correlation between estimated PASP by echocardiography and invasive PASP (r=0.15).

Participants with hemodynamic HFpEF exhibited a steeper rise of both ΔmPAP/ΔCO (4.0 [2.6, 5.0] vs 2.0 [1.5, 2.6] mm Hg·L−1·min−1, p <0.001) and ΔPCWP/ΔCO slopes (3.1 [1.7, 4.2] vs 1.0 [0.7, 1.2] mm Hg·L−1·min−1, p <0.001) with exercise relative to those without HFpEF. However, there were no differences in ΔTPG/ΔCO slope between participants with and without HFpEF (1.0 [0.4, 1.2] vs 0.9 [0.6, 1.5] mm Hg·L−1·min−1, p=0.946), suggestive of predominantly post-capillary contributions to ΔmPAP/ΔCO among participants with HFpEF.22,23

### HFpEF diagnostic scores among those with and without HFpEF

The distribution of both H2FPEF and HFA-PEFF scores were similar between participants with or without HFpEF (Figure 3). Of the 24 participants with confirmed hemodynamic HFpEF, only one individual (4.2%) was categorized as high-risk by HFA-PEFF score, and none were identified as high-risk by H2FPEF score. All participants with HFpEF were categorized as intermediate-risk by H2FPEF, and 21 (87.5%) were classified as intermediate-risk by the HFA-PEFF score. Among participants without hemodynamic HFpEF, none were categorized as high-risk by H2FPEF, whereas 2 (12.5%) were by HFA-PEFF. Similar to the participants with HFpEF, the majority of non-HFpEF participants were categorized as intermediate-risk by both H2FPEF (15, 93.8%) and HFA-PEFF (11, 68.8%) scores.

## DISCUSSION

We found that among adults with obesity, dyspnea, and no known cardiovascular disease, at least a third met hemodynamic criteria for HFpEF on invasive CPET. Moreover, the true prevalence of HFpEF in this sample may be underestimated, given that nearly half of our participants did not undergo CPET. Importantly, our study sample was focused on research volunteers with obesity and undifferentiated dyspnea, rather than patients clinically referred for CPET, highlighting the potential for substantial under-recognition of HFpEF among individuals with obesity and dyspnea in the community. Of note, without invasive hemodynamic evaluation and provocative exercise testing, participants with HFpEF were not clinically distinguishable from those without HFpEF, with similar demographics, comorbidities, NT-proBNP values, and resting echocardiography. Additionally, the majority of participants were deemed intermediate-risk by both the HFA-PEFF and H2FPEF scores, irrespective of HFpEF status. These results not only highlight the high prevalence of undiagnosed HFpEF in the community, but also the limitations of noninvasive HFpEF diagnosis in individuals with obesity.

Our findings corroborate and extend prior work examining the risk of HFpEF among individuals with dyspnea in the community. In a prospective cohort study of patients referred for non-invasive CPET from two multidisciplinary, dedicated dyspnea clinics in Belgium, 15% of patients were identified as high risk for HFpEF by either HFA-PEFF or H2FPEF score and were given a clinical diagnosis of HFpEF.24 Another study of elderly ARIC (Atherosclerosis Risk In Communities) participants without known cardiopulmonary causes of dyspnea used a similar strategy for HFpEF diagnosis, identifying potential HFpEF in up to a third of participants based on a high risk H2FPEF or HFA-PEFF score.25 However, while both studies provided an estimate of HFpEF prevalence based on non-invasive risk score, HFpEF status was not directly ascertained by invasive hemodynamic assessment. In contrast, a much higher estimate of HFpEF prevalence was identified in a study of 461 patients clinically referred for invasive CPET at Massachusetts General Hospital, in which 53% of patients met hemodynamic criteria for HFpEF.3 Our findings build upon and extend these studies by applying rigorous hemodynamic HFpEF ascertainment not just to a population of patients clinically referred for CPET for likely HFpEF, but rather in research participants with obesity and undifferentiated dyspnea, demonstrating that the potential for underdiagnosis of HFpEF is likely magnified in individuals with obesity in the community.

Our findings highlight the challenges and limitations of noninvasive HFpEF diagnosis, particularly amongst individuals with obesity. The universal definition of HF requires a clinical syndrome of HF with an associated structural or functional cardiac abnormality, corroborated by objective evidence of pulmonary or systemic congestion and/or natriuretic peptide elevation.26 However, identification of structural or functional cardiac abnormalities can be challenging in the setting of HFpEF. Resting echocardiographic measures of diastolic dysfunction or adverse cardiac remodeling have variable diagnostic performance in HFpEF; while features such as the peak tricuspid regurgitation velocity, mitral E/A and E/E’ ratio, and left atrial volume index may effectively predict the presence of elevated filling pressures, they may still have poor sensitivity in the diagnosis of HFpEF, particularly in those patients without overt resting congestion.3–5 In the MGH CPET cohort, up to a third of patients with evidence of hemodynamic HFpEF had normal resting echocardiograms.3 Similarly, among patients with HFpEF enrolled in The Prospective Comparison of ARNI [angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitor] with ARB [angiotensin-receptor blockers] Global Outcomes in HF with Preserved Ejection Fraction (PARAGON-HF), 32% had no echocardiographic abnormalities noted.27 The limitations of resting echocardiogram in HFpEF diagnosis may be magnified in obesity due to poor acoustic windows and underestimation of circulatory congestion by echocardiographic hemodynamic markers due to uncoupling between cardiac wall stress and intravascular pressures.10 In our sample, we did not find that traditional resting echocardiographic features discriminated between those with and without HFpEF, with few structural abnormalities overall. Only one participant with HFpEF had an abnormal mitral E/E’ ratio or an elevated pulmonary pressure estimated from tricuspid regurgitation jet, and only a quarter of our HFpEF participants had an abnormal left ventricular wall thickness. Participants with HFpEF were observed to have higher RWT, in keeping with prior studies implicating RWT as an important discriminatory marker between HFpEF and isolated left ventricular hypertrophy.28

Additionally, the diagnostic requirement for natriuretic peptide elevation presents numerous limitations in the diagnosis of HFpEF. Up to a third of individuals with clinical HFpEF may have low or normal natriuretic peptide levels.29 This estimate may be even higher among individuals with HFpEF uncovered on invasive hemodynamic assessment, where up to half may not have natriuretic peptide elevation.3 The limitations of natriuretic peptide assessment are further exacerbated by concomitant obesity in HFpEF, where natriuretic peptide deficiency has been well-described.10,30 Our study corroborates these limitations particularly in the obese population, with 92% of our participants with HFpEF not meeting NT-proBNP biomarker criteria. Overall, our results highlight the inadequacy of resting echocardiogram and natriuretic peptides alone in the evaluation for HFpEF in individuals with obesity.

Multiple strategies to refine non-invasive HFpEF diagnosis have been proposed, including the H2FPEF score and HFA-PEFF diagnostic score algorithms, which integrate clinical, biomarker, and echocardiographic features to evaluate the probability of HFpEF.20,21 Nearly all of our participants were deemed intermediate-risk by both diagnostic scores, with similar score distributions among individuals with and without HFpEF; only one participant was deemed high-risk based on H2FPEF criteria. While diagnostic scores did not discriminate between those with and without HFpEF in our sample, our study highlights the importance of individuals of intermediate-risk by either diagnostic score to be considered for advanced testing including invasive CPET or diastolic stress testing for further diagnostic clarification, as recommended previously.12 Interestingly, individuals with HFpEF in our sample were not clearly distinguishable from those without HFpEF based on non-invasive components of cardiopulmonary exercise testing. Individuals with or without HFpEF had, on average, similarly depressed peak VO2, VE/VCO2 slope, and peak C(a-v)O2, indicating that the common feature of obesity may have been a primary contributor to the impaired cardiorespiratory fitness observed across our sample. This observation also highlights the importance of invasive hemodynamic assessment in the discrimination of HFpEF among individuals with obesity.

Our study demonstrating under-recognition of HFpEF among obese individuals has important clinical implications, as medical therapies for HFpEF are rapidly evolving. The recent approval of SGLT2 inhibitors in HFpEF highlights the importance of early diagnosis and subsequent early medication initiation in the reduction of heart failure hospitalizations and cardiovascular death at a population level.31 Additionally, patients with obesity and HFpEF may also be excellent candidates for early initiation of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonists to reduce body weight and improve both symptom burden and exercise capacity.32,33 The role of these evolving therapies among those without evidence of rest congestion or in the prevention of HFpEF remains to be defined. Lastly, beyond the diagnostic and prognostic role of invasive CPET, the information obtained may also clarify the various contributions of cardiac, respiratory, and peripheral limitations to dyspnea among individuals with HFpEF, with potential to target specific therapies according to phenotype.34,35

Our study has several important limitations. First, our study had a modest sample size which may have limited power to detect between-group differences in clinical and echocardiographic measures. Second, to justify performing invasive CPET on research volunteers who might not otherwise be clinically referred for invasive testing as part of our research protocol, individuals were required to meet strict PASP criteria to qualify for invasive testing. We acknowledge that noninvasive estimation of PASP using PAAT is imperfect, and that the majority of participants had insufficient or absent envelopes for the measurement of tricuspid regurgitation velocity in our sample. Additionally, as we demonstrated, estimated PASP using echocardiographic measures correlates poorly with the presence of pulmonary hypertension and/or HFpEF on invasive testing. In this context, we suspect that perhaps an even greater proportion of our total sample may have unrecognized HFpEF, given that nearly half of our participants did not qualify for CPET in our research protocol. Further, generalizability of our findings is limited in the setting of a modest sample, which could have important implications for HFpEF prevalence, characteristics, and outcomes. Additionally, while we aimed to capture a representative sample of individuals with obesity in the community, the focus on research volunteers could have resulted in self-selection or volunteer bias. Lastly, our study design did not incorporate diastolic stress testing, which could have also helped discriminate the presence of potential HFpEF as an alternative to gold standard hemodynamic diagnosis.36 However, the use of stress echocardiogram is often limited by image quality in individuals with obesity, which may reduce its practicality in this specific population.37

In sum, we highlight that HFpEF is likely under-recognized among individuals with obesity and dyspnea, even in the absence of known CVD. Individuals with HFpEF were not meaningfully distinguishable from those without HFpEF prior to invasive CPET, with similar distributions of clinical characteristics, NT-proBNP levels, resting echocardiogram, and HFpEF diagnostic scores. These findings underscore current diagnostic challenges and potential utility of advanced testing in HFpEF diagnosis, particularly among individuals with obesity. Further, these findings have significant clinical implications as we consider rapidly evolving medical therapies now available for HFpEF. Future investigations focused on HFpEF risk among individuals with obesity to elucidate the role of BMI-specific cutoffs for natriuretic peptide assessment, as well as the identification of other specific biomarkers or non-invasive surrogates of early hemodynamic HFpEF, will be important.38 Additionally, the role of evolving medical therapies in individuals with hemodynamic HFpEF without overt rest congestion remains to be studied.
